overview.text: Auguste Rodin’s bronze sculpture The Thinker shows a muscular, unclothed man leaning forward, his chin resting on his hand and his elbow on a knee. Rodin conceived the figure around 1880 for the top of The Gates of Hell, a monumental doorway inspired by Dante’s Divine Comedy. First called The Poet, it was associated with Dante contemplating the souls in Hell; shown on its own in 1888, it became an independent work. Rodin enlarged it in 1904. Its powerful body and concentrated pose make thinking seem physically demanding, bringing bodily strength together with inward reflection in one of Rodin’s best-known sculptures.

key_facts.text: Rodin first titled the figure The Poet and associated it with Dante; later, it also came to suggest a more universal thinker or creator.
The original figure was about 70 centimeters tall; Rodin exhibited it independently in 1888 and enlarged it in 1904.
The Gates of Hell was commissioned in 1880 as a doorway for a planned Paris museum and drew on Dante’s Divine Comedy, especially the Inferno.
The pose combines a furrowed, thoughtful expression with a tense, muscular body; the National Gallery of Art describes the figure’s chin resting on his hand, with his elbow on his knee.
Rodin’s Gates of Hell was not cast in bronze during his lifetime, while The Thinker became an independent sculpture in multiple casts and sizes.
